items.title: Topology optimization for power grids, on the GPU
items.text:
▶ Take the interactive tour

What is ToOp? | Installation | Quickstart | Usage | How it works

items.title: What is ToOp?
items.text:
Electricity does not take the route we pick for it. It spreads over every line it can reach, simply following the laws of physics. On busy days some of these lines end up carrying more power than they safely can – grid operators call this congestion. The usual fix is redispatch: asking one power plant to produce less and another, somewhere else, to produce more. It works, but it is expensive, and it often means starting up plants that emit more CO₂.

ToOp, short for topology optimization, looks for a cheaper and cleaner way out. Rather than changing who produces the electricity, it changes the layout of the grid itself – for example by switching off a line, or by splitting a substation so that it behaves like two separate junctions. Much like closing a street or opening a new junction in a city, these topological actions gently steer the power away from the lines that are full, and they cost next to nothing to carry out. ToOp searches through the many possible combinations and suggests the most promising ones to the operators in the control room, who always have the final say.

Our goal: help grid operators relieve congestion with clever switching instead of costly redispatch – saving money and CO₂ along the way.

This repository holds the engine behind ToOp at Elia Group. It reads operational grid data through an importer, searches for good topologies in a fast DC optimization stage, and double-checks the best candidates with a full AC validation. It also contains the GPU-based DC load flow solver that makes the search fast. Today ToOp considers transmission line switching, busbar splitting, busbar reassignment and tap optimization of phase-shifting transformers (PSTs).

items.title: Working together
items.text:
We believe topology optimization works best when it is developed jointly and applied to the grid as a whole, taking into account the operational constraints of different TSOs. So please try ToOp, ask questions, share your feedback and your constraints – and if you like it, contribute. We would also love to hear your ideas for combining ToOp with other open-source tools.

  • Contributing: have a look at our contribution guide.
  • Roadmap: see the open feature requests and planned work.
  • Contact: do not hesitate to reach out if you are interested in the project or need help with the setup. Your first point of contact is ToOp@eliagroup.eu.

items.title: Benchmark
items.text:
ToOp comes with a Python file toop-engine-benchmark/benchmark_toop.py to benchmark and profile it. The script supports:

  1. Multirun to sweep across different parameter configurations
  2. Profiling of all stages (Preprocessing, Optimization, Validation)
  3. Insights into the performance of the GPU-based topology optimizer stage:
    • Number of computed injection combinations
    • Number of computed topologies (per epoch)
    • Tensorboard traces to analyze the optimization in-depth
    • Plotting cell distribution of genetic algorithm
  4. Assessment to propose the best parameter configuration using toop-engine-benchmark/assess_benchmark.py, including:
    • Timing metrics across runs for each stage
    • Best run based on metric
    • Best parameter combination

We use the common hydra library for multiruns and configuration parameter optimization. It uses YAML files for its configuration which can be found in toop-engine-benchmark/config/. These files pose the default config with which the benchmark runs.

You can run the a single benchmark with 

uv run python -m toop-engine-benchmark.benchmark_toop
and read the results from the benchmark_summary.json.

In most cases, you probably want to run several benchmarks with different parameters.

items.title: Multirun and parameter sweep
items.text:
If you aim to find the best parameter configuration for ToOp and your grid file(s), you want to run the algorithm with several combinations of parameters. You start a multirun by passing the multirun flag --multirun to hydra. At the project's root directory, we run: 

uv run python -m toop-engine-benchmark.benchmark_toop --multirun grid=config_grid_node_breaker ga_config.runtime_seconds=10,20 ga_config.split_subs=2,5

This will run the benchmark on the grid node breaker example using two different runtimes for the genetic algorithm and two different maximum number of split substations, in total four different combinations. The output directory of the benchmark is configured in toop-engine-benchmark/configs/grid/config_grid_node_breaker.yaml via the output_dir field.

items.title: Extensibility
items.text:
Since ToOp requires a large number of configuration parameters that rarely require tuning but may still investigated, we decided to prioritize usability over exhaustive parameter selection. We restricted the configurable parameters to the subset we deem most relevant to investigate the overall performance.

If you wish to investigate other parameters, you can extend the main loop of toop-engine-benchmark/benchmark_toop.py to support this. You need to perform three steps to extend the set of parameters that can be considered for hyperparameter search: 1. Create (or extend an existing) hydra YAML file with the parameter you would like to include. 2. Extend the main loop of the benchmark to pass the config's new parameter to its corresponding internal config (e.g. ga_config, lf_config etc.). 3. Vary the parameter via CLI multirun (or using hydra experiment configs).

For example, ga_config contains mutation_repetition which determines the number of candidates to mutate during an iteration. One may want to adjust this to steer the algorithm to explore more randomly.

items.title: Assessment
items.text:
We include an assessment script that computes a number of interesting metrics to observe the performance over time. These metrics could be displayed in a health dashboard of the software.

When prompted with a directory of results of a multirun, the assessment script assesses the hyperparameter sweep, providing the best combination found. It also computes timing metrics of each stage of the pipeline.

Let's imagine you have previously run a multirun. You can then assess it via: 

uv run python -m toop-engine-benchmark.assess_benchmarks root=/workspaces/ToOp/data/grid_node_breaker/results/multirun save=/workspaces/ToOp/data/grid_node_breaker/results/aggregate_report.json print=true

items.title: Contributing to ToOp
items.text: Thank you for your interest in contributing to ToOp! This guide will help you understand our development workflow and contribution process.

items.title: Local Development Setup
items.text: Furthermore, we recommend the use of Visual Studio Code as you IDE including its Python Extension for an integrated test environment. If you want to run all tests locally, you also need Docker.

items.title: Getting Started
items.text:
Clone the repository 

   git clone https://github.com/eliagroup/ToOp.git
   cd ToOp
and install dependencies by running 
  uv sync --all-groups

items.title: Test installation
items.text:
VS Code should automatically detect all tests on the Test tab. Alternatively, you can run all tests via the terminal by running 

   uv run pytest
or the test of some package via 
   uv run pytest packages/<package_name>_pkg/tests

items.title: Contributing via Pull Requests
items.text:
We use trunk-based development, where main refers to the stable trunk branch containing all development and releases.

The contribution guidelines differ slightly between internal and external developers. As an external developer, you can fork our repository and contribute to code via pull requests. Make sure to name pull request according to our commit message standard as CI validation will fail otherwise.

items.title: Contributing with AI/LLM tools
items.text:
You may use AI coding assistants, but:

  • You are fully responsible for all contributed code, whether written manually or generated.
  • You must understand and be able to explain every submitted change.
  • A human must always review, validate, and approve the final contribution.
  • Do not use AI to interact with maintainers on your behalf. Improving grammar or clarity of your message is permitted.
  • Fully autonomous AI agents that open PRs without human review are not allowed and PRs will be rejected.

items.title: Acknowledgements
items.text: This AI contribution guide is mainly based on SymPy and SciPy developers' AI policies. We thank them for their contribution.

items.title: Branching for Development
items.text:
You are advised to name branches in accordance with your goal. For that, we provide commit message types. For example, if you develop a new feature you can name your branch:

Feature Development: Create feature branches from main 

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout -b feat/your-feature-name

Bug Fixes: Create fix branches from main 

git checkout main
git pull origin main
git checkout -b fix/fix-description

items.title: Standard PR workflow for external developers
items.text:
1. Fork and install: 

    python3.14 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/ToOp.git
cd ToOp
uv sync
uv run prek install

  2. Add our repo to merge updates: 

    git remote add upstream https://github.com/eliagroup/ToOp.git

  3. Create a branch from main: 

    git checkout main
git pull upstream main
git checkout -b feat/your-change

  4. Implement and validate (tests + checks): 

    uv run pytest
uv run prek run --all-files

  5. Sync with upstream before pushing to your fork: 

    git fetch upstream
git rebase upstream/main

  6. Commit your change: We require Conventional Commits and Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) for each commit to the main branch. Note that these commit messages are based on all commit messages within your PR, which will be squashed before a merge into main. You will make your life easier by adhering to conventional commits throughout all your commits. You can do so by using the -s flag when committing. 

    git add <files>
git commit -s

  7. Push to your fork and open a PR to main: 

    git push --set-upstream origin feat/your-change

items.title: Acceptance Criteria for PRs
items.text:
• Single purpose: Each PR should contain one type of change - either a feature, a bugfix, or a refactor. Avoid mixing different types of changes in a single PR

  • PR description should be meaningful but concise. Use the following template:

  • Title of the pull request must conform to the conventional commit spec. It will be used for the squashed commit message of a PR.

  • Pull request squash commit message has to include Developer Certificate of Origin. Under some circumstances GitHub automatically adds author's signature, but in some cases it has to be added manually.
  • Code must pass all pre-commit hooks uv run prek run --all-files.
  • Tests must pass.
  • Code coverage must be over 90% and aimed for 100%.
  • Test locally by running uv run pytest
  • Documentation should be updated if needed

items.title: PR Commit Message Standards
items.text:
We require Conventional Commits and Developer Certificate of Origin (DCO) for each commit in the main branch. These commits are created when a pull request is squashed into the main branch.

Such a pull request's commit message must follow this format:

<type>[optional scope]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]

Signed-off-by: FirstName LastName <something@example.org>

items.title: Commit Types
items.text:
• feat: A new feature
  • fix: A bug fix
  • docs: Documentation only changes
  • style: Changes that do not affect the meaning of the code
  • refactor: A code change that neither fixes a bug nor adds a feature
  • perf: A code change that improves performance
  • test: Adding missing tests or correcting existing tests
  • chore: Changes to the build process or auxiliary tools

items.title: Developer Certificate of Origin
items.text: The last line of the commit message certifies the origin of the code that will be committed. This means that you certify you have the rights to submit this work under this project's open source license (see Git docs).

items.title: Examples
items.text:
feat: add user authentication system

Signed-off-by: FirstName LastName <something@example.org>
---------------------------------------------------------

fix(api): resolve memory leak in data processing

Signed-off-by: FirstName LastName <something@example.org>
---------------------------------------------------------

docs: update installation instructions

Signed-off-by: FirstName LastName <something@example.org>

items.title: Commit Message Validation
items.text: Commit messages are not validated but the final squashed commit of your PR will be. For that, we use Commitizen with the conventional commits standard.

items.title: Writing tests
items.text: These rules apply to humans and coding agents alike. Ruff does not lint tests/, so reviewers check them by hand.

items.title: Structure
items.text:
• Mirror src/. The test for toop_engine_x/a/b.py lives in packages/x_pkg/tests/a/test_b.py. Look for an existing module before creating a new one.
  • One behaviour per test. Arrange, act, assert. If a test needs a paragraph to explain, or grows past a screen, split it.
  • Name the behaviour, not the function. Use test_<unit>_<does_what>_<when>, so a failing name reads as a bug report.
Good Not good test_screening_is_skipped_when_the_basecase_did_not_converge test_main test_update_static_information_removes_busbar_data_when_disabled test_preprocess_net_step1 test_switching_tables_V2

See contingency_analysis_pkg/tests/pandapower/cascade/test_basecase_screen.py and topology_optimizer_pkg/tests/dc/genetic_functions/test_initialization.py for the style we want. - Assert values. A test must fail when the behaviour breaks. assert True, assert result is not None on its own, or "it did not raise" are not tests. Compare against expected numbers, shapes, ids or a reference implementation (e.g. dc_solver_pkg/tests/numpy_reference.py). - Do not weaken tests to make them pass. Changing an expected value, widening a tolerance, adding skip/xfail or deleting a test needs a reason in the PR description.

items.title: Fixtures
items.text:
• Reuse before you create. Each package's tests/conftest.py already provides grids, preprocessed folders, StaticInformation, N-1 definitions and Kafka setups. Search it before writing a new fixture, and extend an existing one rather than copying it.
  • Expensive data once, copies per test. A session-scoped _name fixture builds the data; a function-scoped name fixture returns a copy, so tests can mutate it safely:
@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def _case14_data_folder(tmp_path_factory: pytest.TempPathFactory) -> Path:
    tmp_path = tmp_path_factory.mktemp("case14")
    case14_pandapower(tmp_path)
    return tmp_path


@pytest.fixture
def case14_data_folder(_case14_data_folder: Path, tmp_path: Path) -> Path:
    shutil.copytree(_case14_data_folder, tmp_path, dirs_exist_ok=True)
    return tmp_path
  • Smallest grid that shows the behaviour. Use case14 or a synthetic network before case57, Oberrhein or real UCTE/CGMES data.
  • Fixture names describe content (case14_data_folder, jax_inputs_oberrhein), never test_*, data1 or ..._V2.

items.title: Cost tiers and the development loop
items.text:
A fast loop lets you, and coding agents, iterate in seconds instead of minutes:

  1. Run the single test you are working on: uv run pytest packages/<pkg>/tests/<path>::<test_name>.
  2. Run its module, then the package: uv run pytest packages/<pkg>/tests.
  3. Run the full suite (uv run pytest -n auto --dist loadgroup) only before opening the PR, or leave it to CI.

Know what a test costs before you add it:

  • Pure unit tests (plain functions, small arrays, case14) should run in well under a second. Prefer this tier.
  • JAX tests pay compilation on first call. Reuse compiled shapes and avoid parametrizing over many shapes. Set JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu without a GPU.
  • Service tests need Docker (Kafka, Ray). Group Kafka tests with @pytest.mark.xdist_group("kafka").
  • Give slow tests an explicit @pytest.mark.timeout(...).

Coverage must stay above 90% (.coveragerc). Treat it as a signal for untested behaviour, not as a target to hit with assertion-free tests.

items.title: Naming & documentation
items.text: Good names make most review comments unnecessary. Before you open a PR, read your diff once only for names.

items.title: Names
items.text:
• Say what it is in domain terms, not how or when it was made. Use the vocabulary from the glossary; do not invent synonyms. Add a new term to the glossary in the same PR.
  • Avoid these patterns (all taken from the current code base):
Pattern Example Better _helper, _utils, do_, process_ with no object graph_creation_nodes_helper add_nodes_to_graph Version or step suffixes basic_node_breaker_network_powsybl_v2, preprocess_net_step1 describe the content: node_breaker_network_with_six_voltage_levels, clean_up_imported_network One variable reused for different things res holding flows, then masked flows, then monitored flows flows, masked_flows, monitored_flows Generic containers df, data, tmp, result branch_results, outage_group_table Single letters outside formulas b = network.get_buses() buses = network.get_buses()
  • Single letters are fine for indices in short loops and for symbols from a formula the docstring cites.
  • Keep the established conventions: n_ prefix for counts and dimensions, _mask for boolean arrays, _ids for string identifiers, from_node / to_node for branch ends, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for module constants.
  • Booleans read as a statement: is_monitored, has_converged, enable_bb_outages.

items.title: Docstrings and comments
items.text:
• Every public function has a NumPy-style docstring with Parameters, Returns and Raises where applicable (ruff.toml: convention = "numpy"). One-line docstrings are fine for small helpers without parameters.
  • Document what the signature cannot say: intent, units (MW, p.u., degrees), array shapes, invariants, and why edge cases are handled the way they are. Do not restate the type hints.
  • Dataclass and Pydantic attributes are documented with a string directly below the field.
  • Comments explain why. If a comment explains what a block does, extract the block into a well-named function instead.
  • When you change behaviour, update the docstring, the relevant docs/ page, the glossary, and the architecture model if cross-package flow changed.

items.title: Release Process
items.text: Releases are managed through GitHub Actions and only generate Git tags. No commits are created during the release process.

items.title: Release Types
items.text:
1. Stable Releases (from main branch):
  2. Follow semantic versioning (e.g., v1.2.3)

  3. Used for production-ready code

  4. Development Releases (from feature branches):

  5. Include a development identifier (e.g., v1.2.3.dev12345)
  6. Used for testing and preview purposes

items.title: Release Workflow
items.text:
The release process is automated through .github/workflows/release.yaml:

  1. Manual Trigger: Releases are triggered manually via GitHub Actions
  2. Version Calculation: Commitizen analyzes commit history to determine the next version
  3. Tag Creation: A Git tag is created with the new version
  4. Tag Push: The tag is pushed to the repository

Note: Releases only create Git tags. No packages are published to external registries.

items.title: Creating a Release
items.text:
1. Ensure your branch has the changes you want to release
  2. Go to the GitHub Actions tab in the repository
  3. Select the "release" workflow
  4. Click "Run workflow" and select the appropriate branch
  5. The workflow will automatically determine the next version and create a tag

items.title: Glossary
items.text:
The shared vocabulary of ToOp, for humans and coding agents alike. Each entry gives a short definition, the identifiers used in code, variants to avoid and, where one exists, the page with the full explanation. The explanation itself lives on that page only.

If you introduce, rename or sharpen a term, update this page in the same pull request.

items.title: Branch
items.text:
A two-terminal element with a from_node and a to_node: line, two-winding transformer, tie line, boundary line. Three-winding transformers are split into branches during preprocessing according to the star-equivalent.

  • Code: NetworkData.branch_ids, from_node, to_node; dimension n_branches; GridElement.kind == "branch"; BranchAsset.
  • Avoid: "line" when transformers are included too.
  • See: DC solver preprocessing.

items.title: Injection
items.text:
A one-terminal element that injects or consumes active power at a node: generator, load, static generator, shunt, external grid, HVDC end. Note that in DC, no PV/PQ differentiation happens, so all injecting elements are treated the same.

  • Code: NetworkData.injection_ids, injection_nodes; DynamicInformation.nodal_injections; GridElement.kind == "injection"; InjectionAsset.
  • Abbreviation: inj.

items.title: Node / bus
items.text:
An electrical node of the bus-branch model. Preprocessing (NetworkData) says node (node_ids, relevant_node_mask); the JAX solver says bus (n_bus in the PTDF). Use whichever the surrounding module uses, consistently.

  • Avoid: "bus" when you mean a physical busbar. Note that in the N-1 definition GridElement.kind == "bus" refers to a busbar section or bus-breaker bus.
  • Note the different naming conventions in pandapower and powsybl. Pandapower has a unified "bus" concept that applies to across bus-branch buses and node-breaker nodes.

items.title: Station / bus group
items.text:
A switchable group of busbars together with the assets connected to them. The asset-topology model calls it a bus group (bus_group_id); one physical substation can contain several structural bus groups (suffixes _a, _b, …). In the solver, a sub is the node of a relevant station with its local branches and injections.

  • Code: MasterBusGroup, RuntimeBusGroup, SimplifiedBusGroup; solver: n_sub_relevant, branches_per_sub, substation_correspondence.
  • Variants in use: station, substation, sub. Prefer bus group in asset-topology code and sub only in solver dimension names.
  • See: Asset topology, bus-group identity.

items.title: Busbar (physical vs electrical)
items.text:
A physical busbar is a Busbar inside a bus group. An electrical busbar is what remains after closed couplers are merged. The optimizer splits a station into at most two electrical busbars, called the A and B side.

  • Code: Busbar, RuntimeBusbar.
  • See: Switching distance.

items.title: Busbar coupler
items.text:
A switch between two busbars of the same bus group. Opening it splits the station; the flow it carried while closed is the cross-coupler flow.

  • Code: BusbarCoupler, RuntimeBusbarCoupler, CouplerBay; mask cross_coupler_limits; metric cross_coupler_flow.

items.title: Asset topology
items.text:
The asset-level (node-breaker) description of stations which consists of busbars, couplers, bays and switching tables. It translates electrical actions into real switch states. - Master is the structural model, independent of switch states. - Runtime is the live switch state. - Simplified is the runtime state projected onto what the DC solver models.

  • Code: MasterAssetTopology, RuntimeAssetTopology, SimplifiedAssetTopology and their *BusGroup classes. AppliedStation, RealizedStation and RealizedTopology are deprecated.
  • Avoid: "AssetTopology" or "Station" as class names; they no longer exist.
  • See: Asset topology.

items.title: PST / parallel PST group
items.text:
A phase-shifting transformer whose tap position is an optimization variable. A parallel PST group is a set of PSTs between the same buses with identical parameters that share one tap change (powsybl grids with enable_parallel_pst_group_optim).

  • Code: PSTRange.pst_group, controllable_pst_indices, Topology.pst_setpoints; metric pst_activated.
  • See: Parallel PST grouping.

items.title: Timestep
items.text: One snapshot of a time series. Arrays carry an n_timesteps dimension; a strategy holds one topology per timestep. Note that currently, timestep support is not fully implemented in ToOp.

items.title: N-0 / base case
items.text:
The grid without any outage. In an N-1 definition it is the contingency with no elements.

  • Code: Nminus1Definition.base_case; suffix _n_0 on metrics; n_0_matrix.
  • See: Metrics.

items.title: N-1 definition
items.text:
The list of contingencies to simulate and the elements to monitor. Contingencies consists of single and multi-outages as well as busbar outages if configured, i.e. literature usually refers to this as N-k. It is stored separately from the grid model. Three forms exist: - The input N-1 definition, which is an authoritative and extensive list of monitored elements and contingencies to consider. - The grid-validated N-1 definition, whose elements have been checked against the grid model (existence in the grid, type of element). - The DC abstraction derived from it for the DC solver, limited to what the DC model can represent.

  • Code: Nminus1Definition (monitored_elements, contingencies), GridElement, MonitoredElement; files input_nminus1_definition.json, nminus1_definition.json, dc_nminus1_definition.json
  • Avoid: "business N-1 definition".
  • See: Data artifacts.

items.title: Contingency / outage / failure / out of service
items.text:
A contingency is one N-1 case: a set of elements taken out of service together. An outage is the act of taking an element out of service.

  • Code: Contingency, contingency_ids; solver: branches_to_fail, dimension n_failures, multi_outage_branches.
  • Prefer: contingency for the business concept, outage for the element being removed, failure only in existing solver dimension names.
  • See: Contingency propagation.

items.title: Outage group
items.text:
The set of elements that are de-energised together because breakers isolate them with a contingency. Several contingencies can map to the same outage group.

  • Code: outage_group_id, element_outage_group_id (loadflow results), apply_outage_grouping.
  • See: Contingency propagation.

items.title: Busbar outage
items.text:
The outage of a physical busbar. It propagates over closed non-breaker couplers and is then expressed as branch outages plus injection changes, without islanding the grid. It can count as an N-1 case or as a separate penalty.

  • Code: SolverConfig.enable_bb_outages, bb_outage_as_nminus1, clip_bb_outage_penalty; RelBBOutageData, NonRelBBOutageData; mask busbar_for_nminus1; metrics bb_outage_*.
  • Abbreviation: bb_outage.
  • See: Busbar outage.

items.title: Monitored element / masks
items.text:
A monitored element is an element whose loadflow results are computed and checked in every contingency. For branches it is the union of optimized and non-worsening branches; only monitored branches appear in loadflow results, limits and metrics. Each monitored element carries a role (optimized, non-worsening), a displayed flag and an overload weight.

The importer writes the same information as boolean and float masks. Naming pattern: *_for_nminus1 (outaged as a contingency), *_for_optimized and *_for_non_worsening (monitored, with that role), *_overload_weight, *_disconnectable, *_blacklisted (excluded from monitoring).

  • Code: MonitoredElement (optimized, non_worsening, displayed, weight, monitoring_scope); NETWORK_MASK_NAMES (folder_structure.py), NetworkMasks; NetworkData.monitored_branch_mask; DynamicInformation.branches_monitored; dimension n_branches_monitored.
  • Avoid: *_for_reward; the masks were renamed to *_for_optimized.
  • See: Monitored branches, Importer masks.

items.title: Optimized / non-worsening branch
items.text:
The role of a monitored branch in the objective. An optimized branch is healed: the optimizer reduces its flow if it exceeds its limit. A non-worsening branch is not healed, but its loading must not get worse than before the optimization. Typical non-worsening branches are border lines, tie lines and DSO transformers. A branch can hold both roles.

The solver does not read the role directly; the role decides the branch's artificial limit.

  • Code: MonitoredElement.optimized, MonitoredElement.non_worsening; masks *_for_optimized, *_for_non_worsening; NetworkData.optimized_branch_mask, non_worsening_branch_mask; BranchLimits.optimized_mask, non_worsening_mask; statistics n_branches_optimized, n_branches_non_worsening.
  • Avoid: "observed" for optimized
  • See: Monitored branches, Artificial limit by branch role.

items.title: Artificial limit / permanent limit
items.text:
The permanent limit is the physical limit of a branch. The artificial limit is the limit the optimizer measures overloads against. The importer derives it per monitored branch from the physical limit, the worst current and the branch role.

  • Code: operational limits permanent_limit, artificial_limit_n_0, artificial_limit_n_1; DoubleLimits (double_limits); solver BranchLimits.max_mw_flow, max_mw_flow_n_1; metric suffixes _permanent_n_*, _artificial_limit_n_*; AC limit_scope.
  • See: Artificial limits, Metrics.

items.title: Displayed element
items.text:
A monitored element that is shown to the user. An element can be monitored only because the optimization needs it as a boundary condition (for example a non-worsening border line) without being of interest to the user. Displaying has no effect on the optimization; it only filters what is reported.

  • Code: MonitoredElement.displayed (default True); displayed_branch_ids; metrics max_flow_displayed_permanent_n_0, max_flow_displayed_permanent_n_1.
  • See: Metrics.

items.title: Overload
items.text:
Flow above a branch limit. Overload energy is the MW above the limit summed over branches and timesteps (for N-1, over the worst contingency).

  • Code: overload_energy_artificial_limit_n_0, overload_energy_artificial_limit_n_1, critical_branch_count, MetricType.
  • See: Metrics.

items.title: Relevant substation
items.text:
A station at which the optimizer may apply split actions.

  • Code: mask relevant_subs; NetworkData.relevant_node_mask; pruned by remove_relevant_subs during DC preprocessing.
  • Caution: the set after DC preprocessing can be smaller than the importer mask (see open questions).

items.title: Split and unsplit
items.text:
A split assigns the branches and injections of a relevant station to two electrical busbars. Unsplit is the original configuration.

  • Code: dimension n_splits; metric split_subs; unsplit_action_mask, unsplit_flow, get_unsplit_ac_topology.

items.title: Branch action / injection action / action set
items.text:
A branch action assigns each branch of one station to busbar A or B; an injection action does the same for injections. The action set holds all allowed actions of all relevant stations. Topologies refer to actions by index into it.

  • Code: two classes share the name ActionSet: the persisted one in stored_action_set.py (file action_set.json) and the JAX one in dc_solver/jax/types.py. Always say which one you mean.
  • See: DC solver preprocessing.

items.title: Disconnection
items.text:
A remedial action that opens a branch. Only branches flagged as disconnectable may be disconnected.

  • Code: masks *_disconnectable; disconnectable_branches; Topology.disconnections; metric disconnected_branches.

items.title: Bridging branch
items.text:
A bridging branch is a branch whose outage islands the grid.

  • Code: bridging_branch_mask, find_bridges, find_n_minus_2_safe_branches, filter_disconnectable_branches_nminus2.
  • See: preprocess() routine.

items.title: Switching distance
items.text:
The number of changes needed to reach a topology from the starting one. Physical distance counts switch operations; electrical distance counts assets assigned to an electrical busbar (electrical node). The optimizer uses the electrical switching distance.

  • Code: metric switching_distance; reassignment_distance; preprocess_switching.py.
  • See: Switching distance.

items.title: Topology / strategy
items.text:
A topology is the set of actions for one timestep: action indices, disconnections and PST setpoints. A strategy is one topology per timestep. The topo-vect format is an alternative flat boolean encoding of branch assignments.

  • Code: Topology, Strategy (optimizer messages), ACStrategy; ActionIndexComputations, TopoVectBranchComputations, convert_branch_topo_vect.

items.title: PTDF / LODF / MODF / BSDF / PSDF
items.text:
Sensitivity matrices of the DC loadflow:

  • PTDF: change of branch flow per nodal injection (n_branches × n_bus).
  • LODF: change of branch flows when a single branch is outaged.
  • MODF: the same for multi-element outages.
  • BSDF: bus split distribution factors, which update the PTDF when a station is split.
  • PSDF: change of branch flow per phase-shifter angle (preprocessing only).

items.title: NetworkData / StaticInformation / DynamicInformation / SolverConfig
items.text:
• NetworkData: NumPy preprocessing state built from a backend.
  • StaticInformation: the solver input, stored as static_information.hdf5. Contains DynamicInformation and SolverConfig.
  • DynamicInformation: traced JAX arrays. Changing values (not shapes) does not trigger recompilation.
  • SolverConfig: static configuration. Changing it triggers recompilation.

Note that StaticInformation contains the dynamic information; the names describe persistence, not traceability.

items.title: DC stage / AC stage
items.text:
The DC stage is a GPU genetic algorithm that searches topologies with the DC loadflow. The AC stage re-validates promising DC topologies with a full AC loadflow.

  • Code: OptimizerType.DC, OptimizerType.AC.
  • See: Deep dive.

items.title: Repertoire and descriptor
items.text:
The DC stage keeps a MAP-Elites repertoire: a grid of cells, each holding the best topology found for one combination of descriptor values. Default descriptors are split_subs and switching_distance.

  • Code: DescriptorDef, me_descriptors; topology_optimizer/dc/repertoire/; file repertoire.json.

items.title: Pull
items.text:
The AC operator that takes a topology from the DC repertoire into the AC stage. It is currently the only AC evolution operator.

  • Code: pull, select_strategy, FilterStrategy (ac/evolution_functions.py).
  • See: Select strategy, AC loop.

items.title: Worst-k contingencies / fast-failing
items.text:
The k contingencies with the highest overload. The AC stage evaluates them first and rejects candidates that already fail there (fast-failing), before running the remaining contingencies.

  • Code: n_worst_contingencies, worst_k_contingency_cases, WorstKContingencyResults, process_fast_failing_results.
  • See: Early stopping.

items.title: Naming conventions in code
items.text:
• Counts and dimensions start with n_ (n_branches, n_timesteps), never num_ or _count.
  • Boolean arrays end in _mask, string identifier lists in _ids.
  • Branch ends are from_node / to_node, not source / target.
  • JAX shape strings reuse existing dimension names; see packages/dc_solver_pkg/AGENTS.md.

items.title: Open questions
items.text:
Terminology the team has not settled yet. Do not pick a side in code; follow the decision once it is recorded here.

  • Element type strings. GridElement.type differs by producer (busbar vs BUSBAR_SECTION, switch kinds vs SWITCH).
  • Relevant / monitored station scope. The importer monitors all stations in relevant_subs, while the DC stage monitors only those still relevant after preprocessing.
  • n_failures. Counts only single-branch outages in some solver arrays and all contingencies in others.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
A ToOp run passes through three stages. Each one is a worker that can also run on its own:

  1. Importer – reads a UCTE or CGMES grid, builds the masks and the N-1 definition, and prepares everything the GPU needs.
  2. DC-Optimizer – a genetic, quality-diversity search on the GPU; every candidate topology is scored with a batched DC load flow.
  3. AC-Validator – picks the most promising candidates and checks them with a full AC contingency analysis before they reach the operator.

For a visual, step-by-step tour of these stages – what every component does and which package implements it – take the interactive tour. The C4 architecture model behind it is described in the architecture overview.

▶ Take the interactive tour

ToOp ships no GUI or system integration: you drive it from Python or through Kafka commands, see Usage.

items.title: High-level architecture
items.text:
ToOp takes operational grid files (for example UCTE or CGMES) as input. They are imported with open-source libraries and normalized into a processed grid folder: the importer writes the backend grid snapshot together with masks, loadflow parameters and topology metadata, and the DC preprocessing adds static_information.hdf5, action_set.json and the final contingency definition.

The preprocessed files are then optimized in a GPU-native set-up: the genetic optimizer together with the GPU-based load flow solver. The results are kept as a Pareto front – a set of solutions where none can be improved in one objective without becoming worse in another. These candidates are validated and filtered with an AC power flow. Finally, a frontend shows the results, so that an operator can review the proposed actions and export the ones they accept to other systems.

items.title: The GPU-based DC load flow solver
items.text:
The GPU-based DC load flow solver computes a large number of similar DC load flows very quickly. It batches over the following dimensions – the workload must not change in anything else:

  • branch topology (the assignment of branches to busbar A or B)
  • injection topology (the assignment of injections to busbar A or B)
  • branch outages

Under the hood it uses PTDF, (G)LODF and BSDF methods. If your workflow fits these requirements, as topology optimization does, the solver can help you too. Read more in the DC solver section.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
ToOp is not published on PyPI yet. Clone the repository and install it with uv:

git clone https://github.com/eliagroup/ToOp.git
cd ToOp
uv sync --all-groups

This installs all six packages of the monorepo together with their dependencies.

items.title: Running on a GPU
items.text:
ToOp runs on a CPU out of the box. To use an NVIDIA GPU, add JAX with CUDA support:

uv pip install "jax[cuda12]"

The DC solver and the genetic search then run on the GPU automatically.

items.title: Using ToOp in your own project
items.text: If your own project uses uv, you can add ToOp as a local dependency in your pyproject.toml, pointing to the cloned repository.

items.title: Setting up for development
items.text:
If you would like to contribute, we recommend the VS Code devcontainer, so that everyone develops in the same environment. You need:

  1. uv
  2. Python 3.14
  3. Visual Studio Code
  4. Docker

The contribution guide walks you through the setup.

items.title: Reading the documentation locally
items.text:
The documentation is built with Zensical:

uv run zensical serve

Then open the address Zensical prints, usually http://localhost:8000.

items.title: Quickstart
items.text: The ToOp repository contains a lot of functionality, which can be overwhelming if you look at it for the first time. But you do not need to understand all of it to use the parts that matter to you. If you would like to grasp the key concepts and data structures first, have a look at Usage. If ToOp is not installed yet, start with the installation guide.

items.title: A batched DC load flow in a few lines
items.text:
Write the IEEE 57-bus test grid to a folder, preprocess it for the GPU solver and compute the flow on every branch:

from pathlib import Path

import jax
from fsspec.implementations.dirfs import DirFileSystem
from toop_engine_dc_solver.example_grids import case57_data_powsybl
from toop_engine_dc_solver.preprocess.convert_to_jax import load_grid, run_initial_loadflow

jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)

folder = Path("data/case57")
case57_data_powsybl(folder)  # write the example grid
stats, static_information, network_data = load_grid(DirFileSystem(str(folder)))

static_information, metrics = run_initial_loadflow(static_information)
print(static_information.dynamic_information.unsplit_flow.shape)  # (timesteps, branches) -> (1, 82)

items.title: The whole pipeline: import, optimize, validate
items.text:
The pipeline helpers take a grid file all the way to AC-validated topologies. On a laptop CPU this takes about a minute:

from pathlib import Path

from omegaconf import DictConfig
from toop_engine_grid_helpers.powsybl.example_grids import create_complex_grid_battery_hvdc_svc_3w_trafo
from toop_engine_interfaces.messages.preprocess.preprocess_commands import (
    AreaSettings,
    CgmesImporterParameters,
    PreprocessParameters,
)
from toop_engine_topology_optimizer.benchmark.benchmark_utils import (
    get_run_dir,
    perform_ac_analysis,
    run_dc_optimization_stage,
    run_preprocessing,
)
from toop_engine_topology_optimizer.dc.main import CLIArgs
from toop_engine_topology_optimizer.interfaces.messages.commons import DescriptorDef
from toop_engine_topology_optimizer.interfaces.messages.dc_params import BatchedMEParameters, LoadflowSolverParameters

# 1. Write a small demo grid
grid_file = Path("data/demo/grid.xiidm")
data_folder = grid_file.with_suffix("")
data_folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
create_complex_grid_battery_hvdc_svc_3w_trafo().save(grid_file)

# 2. Import it and prepare everything the GPU needs
importer_parameters = CgmesImporterParameters(
    grid_model_file=grid_file,
    data_folder=data_folder,
    area_settings=AreaSettings(cutoff_voltage=10, control_area=[""], view_area=[""], nminus1_area=[""]),
)
run_preprocessing(importer_parameters, data_folder, PreprocessParameters())

# 3. Search for good topologies for ten seconds
run_dir = get_run_dir(data_folder / "optimizer_snapshot")
dc_config = DictConfig(
    CLIArgs(
        ga_config=BatchedMEParameters(
            runtime_seconds=10,
            me_descriptors=(
                DescriptorDef(metric="split_subs", num_cells=3),
                DescriptorDef(metric="disconnected_branches", num_cells=3),
            ),
        ),
        lf_config=LoadflowSolverParameters(max_num_splits=2, max_num_disconnections=2),
        fixed_files=(str(data_folder / "static_information.hdf5"),),
        tensorboard_dir=str(run_dir / "tensorboard"),
        stats_dir=str(run_dir / "stats"),
    ).model_dump()
)
dc_config.update(
    task_name="demo",
    num_cuda_devices=0,  # set to 1 to run on a GPU
    omp_num_threads=4,
    xla_force_host_platform_device_count=None,
    double_precision=True,
)
run_dc_optimization_stage(dc_config, run_dir)

# 4. Check the three best topologies with a full AC contingency analysis
ac_config = DictConfig(
    {"n_processes": 1, "k_best_topos": 3, "critical_voltage_jump_percent": 5.0, "critical_va_diff_degree": 20.0}
)
print(perform_ac_analysis(data_folder, run_dir, ac_validation_cfg=ac_config))

Most workflows start like this, by turning a raw grid file into a processed grid folder. The importer creates the backend grid snapshot, masks, loadflow parameters and topology metadata; load_grid then adds static_information.hdf5, action_set.json, action_set_diffs.hdf5 and the final nminus1_definition.json used by the solver and optimizer.

items.title: Roadmap
items.text: We are currently aligning the roadmap. Below you can find the known open feature requests, next to general stabilization and speed-up improvements. If you are interested in a specific feature, please reach out to us.

items.title: Reconnections
items.text: Add reconnection of disconnected lines as an additional optimization action. This extends ToOp's current action space of reassignments, station splits, disconnections and PST taps.

items.title: Curative actions
items.text: Enable curative topology measures as an additional degree of freedom.

items.title: Time-series optimization
items.text:
• V1: Evaluate an optimized topology over multiple consecutive hours and determine for how long it remains beneficial.
  • V2: Introduce true time-coupled optimization, considering dependencies between consecutive time steps.

items.title: Visualization and frontend
items.text: • Open-source frontend: Open-source the frontend of ToOp. Its structure does not have to adhere to the given bulletin.

items.title: Overview
items.text:
There are 6 packages:

  1. Importer: This packages handles grid import and additional data files necessary to perform topology optimization. It relies on the packages PandaPower and PyPowsybl for grid import, which we refer to as backends.
  2. DC Solver: This packages implements an accelerated DC loadflow solver with GPU support.
  3. Topology Optimizer: This package implements a topology optimizer for electrical transmission grids. It uses multi-objective optimization to determine reconfigurations of substations that reduce for example line overloads.
  4. Interfaces: This package provides a set of abstractions and adapters to enable interoperability between different grid modeling tools and data formats.
  5. Grid Helpers: Contains several helping functions to streamline the use of both backends for grid importing.
  6. Contingency Analysis: Allows to run post-optimization evaluation of topologies by passing them back to the backends (PandaPower and PyPowsybl)

ToOp delivers as an output AC validated Optimization results in the form of:

  • The changes needed to get from the base grid to the optimized topology. As a Diff (e.g. dgs format) or a full Grid (e.g. Pandapower or PyPowSyBl)
  • PyPowSyBl only: Two sets of Single Line Diagrams (SLD). The Layout of the Substation before and after the Split.
  • AC and DC load-flow tables before and after the split.
  • A map elites repertoire for AC and DC, with the best topologies picked by the optimizer.

If you want to use all capabilities of this repository, you need to understand how the packages interact and integrate with each other. To see this in action, you can either use the direct python interface or run the whole repo as a composition of Docker containers.

To see the whole repo in action, check out the notebooks/example3_e2e_pipeline.ipynb. If you want to use Kafka workers instead, read on.

items.title: Kafka messaging
items.text:
Work-in-progress

We will extend the usage guide of this package incrementally. For now, please refer to the example notebooks. If you are interested in creating Kafka workers, inspect the interfaces for the Kafka topics and trace their usage.

items.title: Step 1: Prepare a processed grid folder
items.text:
To use the tool, you first create a processed grid folder and then derive the solver artifacts from it. This entails two fundamental steps:

  • The importer preprocessing takes an import command and writes the normalized backend grid file, masks, loadflow parameters, asset topology metadata, importer auxiliary data, and an initial nminus1_definition.json.
  • The load_grid function consumes that processed grid folder and writes the solver-facing artifacts, most notably static_information.hdf5, action_set.json, action_set_diffs.hdf5, static_information_stats.json, and dc_nminus1_definition.json, the DC projection of the importer's contingency definition. The importer's nminus1_definition.json is left unchanged and is what AC contingency analysis reads.

items.title: Step 2: Perform an optimization
items.text:
For this, both the DC optimizer and AC validator should be running at the same time to keep runtime constraints. In principle they could be run one after the other, which would greatly simplify deployment, but as the whole point of this project is to have a fast response, we run them at the same time. Note: The AC optimizer consumes the results of the DC optimizer. Therefore the AC Optimizer should run a bit longer/after to be able to consume the latest DC tppologies.

This is set up through kafka messaging. For the beginning we will run everything on the same machine, but in principle you can deploy this on a cluster.

First, set up kafka with 

cd dev-deployment
docker-compose up

This will spin up a kafka server with 6 topics, 3 importer topics and 3 optimizer topics. The importer topics are only required in case you want to run the importer as a kafka component, but they do no harm if you just want to run an optimization. For the optimizer, we have commands which is a topic where usually only an StartOptimizationCommand will be sent to. Also there is the results topic, which contains topologies with their metrics. Both the DC and AC stage push their topologies there, and the AC stage also pulls DC topologies for validation.

Now, we need to spin up the DC and AC optimizer:

cd packages/topology_optimizer_pkg/dc/worker
python3 worker.py --processed_gridfile_folder=/path/to/your/import/

cd packages/topology_optimizer_pkg/ac/
python3 worker.py --processed_gridfile_folder=/path/to/your/import/

They should connect to the kafka that was spun up earlier on their own, you should see new consumers in the kafka logs.

Now, we need to send an optimization command and listen for results.

items.title: Wall of shame
items.text: Known shortcuts that might lead to issues later on / bugs we did not have time to fix yet.

items.title: Busbar outage articulation nodes
items.text: Busbar outages that would split a node are currently excluded from the busbar outages. This could lead to

items.title: Islanding branches
items.text: Islanding branches are currently excluded from the n-1 analysis, because the lodf can not deal with it

items.title: AC runs on reduced outages
items.text: Since the dc solver cant compute all outages (see islanding) some are excluded from the N-1 that is also used in AC.

items.title: AC Topologies that improve convergence rate, but make overload worse are rejected in AC
items.text: If we have a topology that improves the grid situation in a way, that an outage at least converges but shows even more overloads, this topology is excluded although the situation might have been improved. We just did not know about the overloads in AC before.

items.title: powsybl NO_CALCULATION is treated as not successful
items.text: in the AC contingency analysis NO_CALCULATION-status is treated as not successful, although this could also mean branch-was-already-disconnected or other things. This has to be evaluated.

items.title: Architecture diagrams
items.text:
Architecture-as-code for the ToOp engine, written in LikeC4. The .c4 files here are the source of truth; everything else is generated.

Browse the diagrams online — the interactive app, published with the docs for the newest release. Pan, zoom, search, and click into any nested element.

For a lighter, narrated tour of the same pipeline, open the interactive tour, docs/tour/index.html: a standalone page with no build step that walks input → importer → DC-Optimizer → AC-Validator → results, with an animated sketch per component and the package dependency graph.

items.title: Start the viewer
items.text:
./scripts/serve_architecture_diagrams.sh

Then open http://localhost:5173. Every view is browsable with search and click-through navigation, and editing a .c4 file reloads the browser. Ctrl-C stops it.

Docker is the only requirement — no Node toolchain. The devcontainer forwards 5173 and the live-reload port 24678. If 5173 is taken, pass another one and the URL follows: ./scripts/serve_architecture_diagrams.sh docs/architecture 5199.

To build the published app locally instead of serving it: ./scripts/build_architecture_app.sh, then open docs/architecture/app/index.html.

items.title: What is where
items.text:
Each view answers one question. Start with overview.

View Answers overview What does a ToOp run actually do, start to finish? parameters Where is this limit / weight / threshold configured? dataFlow What talks to what, over which technology, carrying what? importerInternals What happens to a grid file, in what order? nminus1Journeys How is the N-1 definition built, with and without an input N-1 definition? dcWorkerInternals How do repertoire, mutation, scoring and the GPU solver fit together? acValidatorInternals How does a DC candidate get selected, checked and accepted? contingencyAnalysis What can pandapower and PyPowSyBl each do, and what does each fill in? assetTopology How does a topology travel from the grid file to an export? loadflowFormat What is inside a stored loadflow folder? index Everything at one level.

In contingencyAnalysis, color carries meaning: green works on both backends, amber is pandapower only, violet is PyPowSyBl only.

Boxes that map onto a module or function link to the published API reference, so you can click from a diagram straight to the docstring.

The model itself is split by concern:

specification.c4        element kinds, tags, colors
model/
  01-externals.c4       who drives the engine, what goes in and out
  02-messaging.c4       Kafka and its topics
  03-storage.c4         the three filesystems and their contents
  04-engine.c4          the ToOp system; every file below extends it
  05..07                one per stage: importer, DC optimizer, AC validator
  08..10                shared packages: contingency, interfaces, postprocess
  11-relations.c4       every relation, grouped by the stage that drives it
  12-parameters.c4      the parameter object each stage takes
views/                  one file per view, numbered as listed above

items.title: Reading more about C4
items.text:
• c4model.com — the C4 model: context, container, component, code. Worth ten minutes before editing the model.
  • likec4.dev — LikeC4, the DSL and viewer used here.
  • likec4.dev/docs — DSL reference, for when you need the exact syntax of a view predicate or a style rule.

items.title: Cascade Simulation
items.text: After each converged contingency load flow, an optional cascade simulation can be enabled via CascadeConfig. It models how a single outage can trigger a chain of further trips through distance protection or current overload.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
Each call to run_single_outage follows this pipeline:

flowchart TD
    INPUT(["⚡ run_single_outage<br/>─────────────────<br/>net · contingency · ctx"])

    subgraph PF["① INITIAL POWER FLOW"]
        direction LR
        OUTAGE["Disconnect<br/>Outaged Elements"]
        SPPS["SpPS<br/>Iteration"]
        LF["pandapower<br/>runpp"]
        OUTAGE --> SPPS --> LF
    end

    subgraph RESULTS["② COLLECT RESULTS"]
        direction LR
        BR["Branch Results<br/>loading · power · per-side"]
        NR["Node Results<br/>voltages"]
        SR["Switch Results<br/>bus-side oriented"]
        RR["Regulating<br/>Element Results"]

        BR ~~~ NR
        NR ~~~ SR
        SR ~~~ RR
    end

    subgraph META["③ METADATA TABLES"]
        direction LR
        SPPSRES["SpPS Results<br/>schemes · iterations"]
        CONV["Convergence<br/>converged / failed"]

        SPPSRES ~~~ CONV
    end

    subgraph CASCADE["④ CASCADE SIMULATION ── NEW"]
        direction TB

        GUARD{"Load flow<br/>converged?<br/>+<br/>CascadeConfig<br/>present?"}

        subgraph CTX["Build Context"]
            BCTX["Relay data<br/>+ Network topology<br/>+ Breaker map"]
        end

        subgraph DETECT["Detect Triggers"]
            DT["Distance Protection<br/>Impedance vs. polygon zones<br/>⚠ WARNING 🟠 ALARM 🔴 DANGER"]
            OL["Current Overload<br/>loading% vs. threshold"]
        end

        EMPTY(["∅ No cascade"])

        subgraph LOOP["Cascade Loop ── up to depth_limit steps"]
            direction TB

            L1["Map triggers → Outage Groups<br/>relay protected elements · connected components"]
            L2["Generate CascadeEvents<br/>element · reason · loading · impedance"]
            L3["Re-run SpPS + Load Flow<br/>(accumulated outages)"]
            L4["Attach SpPS activation info"]
            L5{"More<br/>triggers?"}
            L6{"Load flow<br/>converged?"}
            FAIL(["Failure Event<br/>→ stop"])

            L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L4 --> L5
            L5 -->|yes| L6
            L6 -->|no| FAIL
            L6 -->|yes| L1
        end

        TABLE["Build Cascade Results"]

        GUARD -->|no| EMPTY
        GUARD -->|yes| CTX
        CTX --> DETECT
        DETECT -->|no triggers| EMPTY
        DETECT -->|triggers found| L1
        L5 -->|no| TABLE
        FAIL --> TABLE
        EMPTY --> TABLE
    end

    OUTPUT(["📦 Build LoadflowResults"])

    INPUT --> PF
    PF --> RESULTS
    RESULTS --> META
    META --> CASCADE
    CASCADE --> OUTPUT

    style INPUT fill:#dcfce7,stroke:#10b981,color:#064e3b
    style OUTPUT fill:#ede9fe,stroke:#7c3aed,color:#1e1b4b

items.title: Trigger types
items.text: Type Detection Threshold Current overload Branch loading exceeds the threshold resolved for its element type and case Configurable per CascadeConfig Distance protection Relay impedance falls inside any of the three polygon zones Defined per relay in the relay table

items.title: Current overload thresholds
items.text:
loading is the per-unit ratio i / i_max, so 1.5 means 150 %. The comparison is strict: a branch loaded at exactly its threshold does not trip.

Each branch result row gets its own threshold, resolved from the element type (line, transformer, or anything else) and from whether the row belongs to the base case or to a contingency:

These live on CascadeConfig.overload, an OverloadConfig:

Row Threshold Falls back to line, base case overload.basecase_line overload.current_loading_threshold line, contingency overload.contingency_line overload.basecase_line, then overload.current_loading_threshold trafo / trafo3w, base case overload.basecase_transformer overload.current_loading_threshold trafo / trafo3w, contingency overload.contingency_transformer overload.basecase_transformer, then overload.current_loading_threshold any other table (e.g. impedance) overload.current_loading_threshold —

All four overrides are optional. When none of them are set, every branch is compared against current_loading_threshold, exactly as before they existed.

Unlike the distance-protection factors, these keep their fallback chain: the scalar current_loading_threshold is the value every row uses until a more specific one is set.

items.title: Base-case screening
items.text:
A base case that already violates makes every contingency cascade meaningless: the cascade would start from an already-broken state, and practically every contingency would report one.

Before any contingency is computed, the solved N-0 network is therefore screened once with the same overload and distance-protection detection the simulator uses. Any of the three zones counts as a violation — each means the relay is already reading into its protection characteristic in N-0.

When the base case violates:

  • cascade simulation is skipped for every contingency;
  • the violation is reported instead, as cascade_results rows under the BASECASE contingency with cascade_number = 0. They carry the ordinary CURRENT_VIOLATION / DISTANCE_PROTECTION reasons — the step number is what sets them apart, since simulated cascade events always start at step 1;
  • a warning is added to LoadflowResults.warnings;
  • the N-1 load flows themselves are unaffected — branch, node, switch and va-diff results are computed exactly as usual.

Screening is controlled by stop_cascade_on_basecase_violation (default True). Set it to False to restore the previous behavior and simulate the cascade even from a violating base case — for example in tests that deliberately overload the base case to force a cascade.

The screen is skipped when the base-case load flow did not converge: its res_* tables are stale, so there is nothing meaningful to check.

items.title: Configuration
items.text:
Cascade screening is opt-in. Pass a CascadeConfig instance when building the analysis context:

from toop_engine_contingency_analysis.pandapower.cascade.configuration import (
    CascadeConfig,
    DistanceProtectionConfig,
    DistanceProtectionFactors,
    OverloadConfig,
)

cascade_cfg = CascadeConfig(
    depth_limit=5,
    min_island_size=10,
    overload=OverloadConfig(current_loading_threshold=1.0),
    distance_protection=DistanceProtectionConfig(
        alarm=DistanceProtectionFactors(
                basecase_line=1.0,
            basecase_transformer=1.0,
            basecase_bus_coupler=1.0,
            contingency_line=1.0,
            contingency_transformer=1.0,
            contingency_bus_coupler=1.0,
        ),
        warning=DistanceProtectionFactors(
                basecase_line=1.41,
            basecase_transformer=1.41,
            basecase_bus_coupler=1.41,
            contingency_line=1.41,
            contingency_transformer=1.41,
            contingency_bus_coupler=1.41,
        ),
    ),
    cascade_log_elements=["line", "trafo", "trafo3w"],
    stop_cascade_on_basecase_violation=True,  # skip the cascade when N-0 already violates
)

To trip lines at 150 % and transformers at 180 % instead, add the per-type overrides (see Current overload thresholds):

cascade_cfg = CascadeConfig(
    depth_limit=5,
    min_island_size=10,
    overload=OverloadConfig(
        current_loading_threshold=1.0,  # still used for e.g. impedances
        basecase_line=1.5,
        basecase_transformer=1.8,
    ),
    distance_protection=DistanceProtectionConfig(
        alarm=DistanceProtectionFactors(
                basecase_line=1.0,
            basecase_transformer=1.0,
            basecase_bus_coupler=1.0,
            contingency_line=1.0,
            contingency_transformer=1.0,
            contingency_bus_coupler=1.0,
        ),
        warning=DistanceProtectionFactors(
                basecase_line=1.41,
            basecase_transformer=1.41,
            basecase_bus_coupler=1.41,
            contingency_line=1.41,
            contingency_transformer=1.41,
            contingency_bus_coupler=1.41,
        ),
    ),
    cascade_log_elements=["line", "trafo", "trafo3w"],
)

items.title: Distance protection factors
items.text: A factor divides the relay impedance measurement before the polygon test (x = |r_ohm| / factor), so a larger factor moves the measured point toward the origin and widens the effective area. 1.0 leaves the relay polygon exactly as the relay defines it.

items.title: The three zones
items.text:
A measurement falls into one of three nested zones. DistanceProtectionSeverity names them, innermost first:

Zone What it is Configurable DANGER The relay polygon exactly as the relay defines it — the real trip boundary No. No factor may widen it ALARM The ring just outside the danger polygon distance_protection.alarm WARNING The outermost ring distance_protection.warning

They nest — danger inside alarm inside warning — which in factor terms means 1.0 <= alarm <= warning on each axis. Nothing enforces that: a narrower warning area still works, because a relay inside its raw polygon trips on the danger zone regardless.

A relay trips when it is inside any zone; the severity recorded on the event is the innermost zone it reached. So the warning factors are normally what decide which relays trip, while the alarm factors only move the ALARM/WARNING labeling boundary.

DistanceProtectionConfig holds one DistanceProtectionFactors group per configurable zone, and each group carries every case/element combination:

line transformer bus_coupler base case basecase_line basecase_transformer basecase_bus_coupler contingency contingency_line contingency_transformer contingency_bus_coupler

Six per zone, so twelve in total, all required — none has a default and none falls back to another. A configuration therefore always states the factor it wants on every axis, and a caller written against an older release fails at construction instead of silently picking up a default.

The trip boundary is not configurable

The danger zone is the relay polygon untouched, so no setting here can make the simulation report a trip inside a boundary the physical relay would not cross. Only the two outer screening rings take factors.

A relay whose protection_element is None — it protects elements of more than one type — takes the largest of the three factors, so an ambiguous relay is screened at least as widely as any candidate would screen it.

When cascade is None in the context, the cascade step is skipped and LoadflowResults.cascade_results is an empty DataFrame.

items.title: Relay input: RelaySchema
items.text:
Distance protection needs the relays, passed to the contingency analysis as their own table next to the network — they are not attached to it:

lf_results = run_contingency_analysis_pandapower(
    net=net,
    n_minus_1_definition=nminus1_def,
    job_id="job",
    timestep=0,
    cfg=cfg,
    relays=relays,  # pandas DataFrame validated against RelaySchema
)

Relays are separate from switches. A relay measures at a breaker, but one breaker can carry several relays guarding different elements — a line relay and a transformer relay, say — and one relay can guard several elements, such as two lines.

The table has one row per relay. RelaySchema (toop_engine_contingency_analysis.pandapower.cascade.configuration) defines it, and every column is required:

Column Type Description relay_id str ID of the relay. A relay on several breakers has a row per breaker with the same ID; a trip of any of them takes out the elements of all its rows relay_name str or None Human-readable relay name, copied into the cascade results breaker_uuid str The breaker the relay measures at; matched against net.switch["origin_id"]. Several relays may share one relay_side str Side of the breaker the relay is on: "bus" or "element". Switch results are measured from the bus side, so an "element" relay reads the breaker measurement flipped and a "bus" relay as measured protected_elements list[str] External IDs (origin_id) of the elements the relay protects — lines, trafo or trafo3w. At least one. A trip takes them out, each with the contingency outage group it belongs to protection_element str or None Type of the protected elements, which picks the global factors: "line", "trafo", or None when the relay protects elements of more than one type angle float Opening angle of the protection zone polygon (degrees) r_i float Inner resistance reach of the danger zone (Ω) r_v float Outer resistance reach of the danger zone (Ω) x_v float Outer reactance reach of the danger zone (Ω) custom_base_alarm float Per-relay alarm factor for the base case; NaN falls back to the global factor custom_base_warning float Per-relay warning factor for the base case; NaN falls back to the global factor custom_contingency_alarm float Per-relay alarm factor after a contingency; NaN falls back to the global factor custom_contingency_warning float Per-relay warning factor after a contingency; NaN falls back to the global factor

The table is validated and prepared once per run, then shared read-only by every outage. A missing column, an unknown relay_side or an empty protected_elements list is rejected with a pandera SchemaError. Each protected element ID is resolved to its pandapower rows: an ID that matches several rows (e.g. a line split into segments) protects all of them, and an ID found nowhere is logged and ignored.

Example — a breaker carrying a line relay and a transformer relay, and a relay guarding two lines:

import pandas as pd

zone = {
    "angle": 80.0,       # degrees
    "r_i": 2.5,          # Ω
    "r_v": 10.0,         # Ω
    "x_v": 15.0,         # Ω
    "custom_base_alarm": float("nan"),      # no override -> global alarm factor
    "custom_base_warning": 0.9,
    "custom_contingency_alarm": float("nan"),
    "custom_contingency_warning": 0.9,
}
relays = pd.DataFrame([
    {**zone, "relay_id": "R1", "relay_name": "Q1 line", "breaker_uuid": "breaker-1",
     "relay_side": "element", "protected_elements": ["line-A"], "protection_element": "line"},
    {**zone, "relay_id": "R2", "relay_name": "Q1 trafo", "breaker_uuid": "breaker-1",
     "relay_side": "element", "protected_elements": ["tr-1"], "protection_element": "trafo"},
    {**zone, "relay_id": "R3", "relay_name": "Q7", "breaker_uuid": "breaker-7",
     "relay_side": "bus", "protected_elements": ["line-B", "line-C"], "protection_element": "line"},
])

# net.switch must have an "origin_id" column naming each breaker

Without relays, distance protection triggers are skipped and only current overload is checked.

items.title: What a relay trip takes out
items.text:
A tripping relay takes out the elements it protects, the way a contingency on them would: each protected element goes out together with the whole contingency outage group it belongs to. The breaker the relay sits on, and the side of it, play no part: they only decide how the relay reads the breaker measurement (relay_side). In the example, when R1 trips, line-A goes out with its outage group; tr-1, protected by R2, goes out only if it is in that group.

  • A relay on several breakers takes out the elements of every one of its rows.
  • An element taken out by several relays in one step is reported once, credited to the relay that reached the innermost zone.
  • Protected elements the network does not have are logged and ignored.

items.title: Inspecting the resolved factors
items.text:
describe_relay_zones answers "what will this configuration actually apply to each relay" without running a load flow. Pass the relay table and the config, get one row per relay with its polygon and the factor that each zone and case resolves to:

from toop_engine_contingency_analysis.pandapower.cascade.detection import describe_relay_zones

described = describe_relay_zones(relays, cascade_cfg)

It returns a copy of the relay table with every original column kept, plus:

Column Description poly The protection polygon, built from angle, r_i, r_v and x_v effective_alarm_basecase, effective_alarm_contingency Effective alarm factor for each case effective_warning_basecase, effective_warning_contingency Effective warning factor for each case

angle comes back in radians. This is exactly the table prepare_relays hands to every outage, so the preview and the run see the same values.

The factors are resolved by the same code the cascade uses, so what you see is what a run applies: per-relay overrides are already folded in, and a relay with no protection_element already shows the maximum described above. The danger zone has no column, because its factor is always 1.0.

The input frame is not modified. angle is read in degrees.

items.title: Output
items.text:
Cascade events are stored in LoadflowResults.cascade_results. Each row describes one element trip at one cascade step.

Index columns (uniquely identify each row):

Column Description timestep Timestep of the contingency calculation contingency Unique ID of the contingency that started the cascade cascade_number Cascade step number (0 = pre-existing base-case violation, 1 = first trip after the initial outage, 2 = next, …) element_mrid External identifier of the tripped element

Data columns:

Column Description element_id Internal unique ID of the tripped element element_name Human-readable name of the tripped element element_outage_group_id ID of the outage group the tripped element belongs to contingency_name Human-readable name of the originating contingency contingency_outage_id Outage group ID of the originating contingency cascade_reason Why the element tripped: CURRENT_VIOLATION, DISTANCE_PROTECTION or FAILED_LF loading Branch loading value that caused the trip (current overload events) r_ohm Relay resistance measurement at trip time (distance protection events) x_ohm Relay reactance measurement at trip time (distance protection events) distance_protection_severity Innermost zone reached: DANGER, ALARM or WARNING (distance protection events) relay_id The relay whose trip took the element out (distance protection events) relay_name Human-readable name of that relay (distance protection events) activated_schemes_per_iter SpPS schemes that activated during this cascade step (JSON string)

items.title: Base-case violation rows
items.text:
When base-case screening trips, cascade_results holds only the base-case report. Those rows differ from simulated cascade events:

Column Value cascade_number 0 — found before the first cascade step runs. This is what identifies a base-case row: simulated events always start at 1 contingency, contingency_name, contingency_outage_id BASECASE — the violation belongs to N-0, not to any contingency cascade_reason The ordinary CURRENT_VIOLATION / DISTANCE_PROTECTION reasons element_outage_group_id None — nothing is simulated, so no outage group is computed loading Base-case loading, on the most heavily loaded side of the element r_ohm, x_ohm, distance_protection_severity Base-case relay measurement, as for a simulated relay trip element_mrid, relay_id (distance protection) The breaker whose relay reads into a zone. A breaker with several such relays is reported once, credited to the relay that reached the innermost zone

To find them:

cascade_results.filter(pl.col("cascade_number") == 0)

items.title: Contingency Analysis
items.text: The Contingency Analysis package provides the implementation to the Load-flow-Service interface. This enables a backend independent Contingency definition. Additional it offers either Polars or Pandas DataFrames as a return value.

items.title: Usage:
items.text:
• Run the N-1 analysis on a pypowsybl network with the function get_security_analysis_results.
  • Compute metrics (polars only) for the results using compute_metrics
  • Direct entrypoint for PyPowSyBl: run_contingency_analysis_powsybl
  • Direct entrypoint for Pandapower: run_contingency_analysis_pandapower
  • The contingency definition used downstream is first created during importer preprocessing and then refreshed during load_grid after preprocessing filters have been applied.
  • Manually: Create a converter from you Contingency list to the Nminus1Definition

items.title: Contingency analysis from the powsybl limit violation table
items.text:
run_contingency_analysis_powsybl_violation_table in toop_engine_contingency_analysis.pypowsybl_limit_table is the successor of run_contingency_analysis_powsybl. It runs the same powsybl security analysis, but it reads the limit violation table instead of monitoring elements.

It does not replace the monitored element runner everywhere: the table only holds the elements beyond a limit, so whatever needs the flows of every monitored branch for every contingency keeps run_contingency_analysis_powsybl. That is the importer, which derives the artificial limits from the worst N-1 current of every branch, and the validation of the DC solver against the full N-1 flow matrix.
path: Contingency analysis from the powsybl limit violation table

items.title: Limit violations
items.text:
The violation table of powsybl is returned as it is, split in three fields of LoadflowResults and LoadflowResultsPolars, all following LimitViolationSchema (indexed by timestep, contingency, element, side, limit_type and limit_name in pandas):

  • branch_violations: the CURRENT, ACTIVE_POWER and APPARENT_POWER violations of branch sides,
  • va_diff_violations: the LOW_VOLTAGE_ANGLE and HIGH_VOLTAGE_ANGLE violations, keyed by the voltage angle limits defined on the network (Network.create_voltage_angle_limits, this library does not create them),
  • node_violations: every other violation, e.g. LOW_VOLTAGE and HIGH_VOLTAGE keyed by voltage level.

The base case violations are in these tables as well, next to the monitored base case results.
path: Contingency analysis from the powsybl limit violation table

items.title: Monitored elements
items.text:
The monitored elements of the N-1 definition are translated exactly like for run_contingency_analysis_powsybl. They are monitored for the base case only, so the base case branch, node and regulating element results and the branch limits of both runners match.

Powsybl reports the violations of every element with limits. They are reduced to the monitored elements:

Table Kept branch_violations the monitored lines, tie lines, two and three winding transformers node_violations the voltage levels holding at least one monitored bus va_diff_violations all, they come from angle limits defined on the network on purpose

Apart from that, no row is converted or dropped. A violation of a temporary limit carries that limit. A loading column is added, with a magnitude of 1 at the violated limit:

Limit type loading CURRENT, ACTIVE_POWER, APPARENT_POWER abs(value) / limit, against the reported limit, which may be temporary HIGH_VOLTAGE (value - nominal_v) / (limit - nominal_v), like vm_loading LOW_VOLTAGE (value - nominal_v) / (nominal_v - limit), negative LOW_VOLTAGE_ANGLE, HIGH_VOLTAGE_ANGLE value / limit

Other limit types have no loading. side keeps the powsybl naming: ONE, TWO or THREE for branch sides, empty for voltage and angle violations. Pre-contingency violations carry the base case id. If the N-1 definition has no base case, they are dropped like the base case rows of the other tables.
path: Contingency analysis from the powsybl limit violation table

items.title: Metrics
items.text:
compute_metrics takes the N-0 metrics from the monitored base case, like for run_contingency_analysis_powsybl. The N-1 branch metrics come from the CURRENT violations of branch_violations if the results have a violation table, see LoadflowResultsPolars.uses_limit_violations and get_branch_results_for_metrics. The monitored runner leaves the table None, the violation runner always sets it, so an empty table means no N-1 overload.

A branch side is reported once its current exceeds its lowest limit times the limit reduction. The artificial limits are temporary current limits below the permanent limit, so every overload against the permanent or an artificial limit is in the table. The loading is computed from the reported current against each limit of branch_limits.

N-1 metric From the violation table overload_current_*, critical_branch_count_* same as the monitored run max_flow_* same as the monitored run if a branch is reported, 0.0 otherwise, like for a result filter max_va_diff_n_1, critical_va_diff_count_n_1, voltage_jump_count_n_1 None, the table has no angle differences of the monitored switches and no voltages within the limits

Powsybl reports an N-1 violation that already exists in N-0 only if it grew by more than the flow threshold of the increased violation parameters, i.e. if post > pre * (1 + threshold). get_default_security_analysis_parameters sets the flow threshold to -1, so every N-1 flow violation is reported, also one that is equal to or lower than in N-0. A negative threshold is outside of the range powsybl documents (positive), but it is not validated. With a threshold of 0 or more, an element overloaded in N-0 that no contingency increases has no N-1 violation, so its N-1 overload is missing from the metrics. Powsybl's own default is 0.1.
